title: Leadville North Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Leadville North wells have a 120-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $13,800-$24,000.
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Leadville North means understanding the local well records before you rely on a seller’s description. Within 5 miles, Colorado DWR records show 1,374 permitted wells. Of those, 840 are recorded as constructed, 890 report total depth, 371 report pump yield, and 88 report static water level.

This area is primarily fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The records point to generally moderate well depths and useful yields, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for your lot. Location, fractures, casing, grout, access, and the exact drilling target still matter.

sections.heading: Leadville North well depth and mountain geology
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Leadville North is 120 feet. The middle half runs from 73 to 162 feet, meaning many drilling bids should be based on a relatively shallow well, while still allowing for variation. The 90th-percentile depth is 225 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 860 feet.

Depth records show that 37% of wells are under 100 feet and 59% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 3% are between 300 and 600 feet, and no recorded wells are in the 600-plus-foot category. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 1,304 wells do so, compared with 38 alluvial wells. Fractured granite and gneiss can produce water unevenly, so nearby depth data is useful for planning but cannot promise the same result.

sections.heading: How much water Leadville North wells produce
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. That is a solid local starting point for a household-water discussion, but it is not the same as guaranteed continuous production. The permit records include yield reports for 371 wells, so the yield sample is smaller than the full well population.

Seventy-five percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 15% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Ten percent fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are recorded under 1 gallon per minute. Storage tanks can help a lower-yield well meet household demand. An exempt household-use well also has a 35 gpm pumping limit, and the permit’s allowed use still controls what you can do.

sections.heading: Leadville North water levels and recent measurements
sections.html:
Among the 88 wells reporting static water level, the median depth to water is 70 feet below the ground surface. The middle half is 54 to 110 feet. This gives a useful expectation for pump planning and trench layout, but static water level is not the same as pumping level. A driller still needs to account for drawdown, seasonal conditions, and the completed well’s performance.

The decade series shows a small shift from a 70-foot median in the 2010s to 75 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water was measured slightly deeper in the newer group, but the available measurements are limited and do not establish a broad declining trend by themselves. Ask for the original well construction and pumping information rather than relying only on the map’s general water-level pattern.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Leadville North, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity extends across several decades. Records show 26 permits from the 1960s, 154 from the 1970s, 133 from the 1980s, 277 from the 1990s, 284 from the 2000s, 122 from the 2010s, and 93 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. The mix includes 78% domestic or household wells, 12% monitoring wells, 2% stock wells, and 1% irrigation wells.

The most common driller names in the records are Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne, with 344 wells; Twin Lakes Drilling Co., associated with Schaffer, James O, with 102; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc., associated with Shelton, Steve, with 80. These records identify past permit activity, not a guarantee of current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the written scope directly before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new well costs in Leadville North
sections.html:
Fractured mountain bedrock raises the importance of access, setup, casing, grout, and the final well design. The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 120-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $7,800 to $12,000.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,800 to $24,000 at that median depth. That is a planning range, not a fixed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, difficult trenching, power work, storage, treatment, or a dry-hole outcome can change the total. Ask each driller what is included, how depth is charged, and what happens if the first water-bearing fracture does not produce enough.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building
sections.html:
The records show 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,848 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are reasons to review location-specific history and test the water. Historic mining can also complicate access, excavation, and site planning.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured bedrock, even when nearby wells look good. Check well construction, casing, grout, pump tests, water-quality results, and maintenance records. For a new build, confirm the well location and septic area can meet required separation and siting rules. A permit, septic approval, and legal water use are separate questions. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be needed, so verify the water-rights requirements with Colorado DWR before construction.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Leadville North
sections.html:
Start with the closest comparable wells, giving priority to wells in the same bedrock setting and at similar elevations. Compare depth, reported yield, static water level, construction, and well use. Leadville is about 1 mile away; Alma is 13 miles away, Copper Mountain 16 miles, Fairplay 17 miles, Red Cliff 18 miles, and Norrie 19 miles. Those places provide context, but the closest comparable well is usually more useful than a distant average.

Before closing, obtain the permit and construction records, confirm the intended household use, and have the existing well tested if the property has one. For vacant land, get a driller’s access and depth estimate, locate power and septic areas, and budget for the full finished system rather than only the hole. If the home will need more water than ordinary household use, check the permit and water-rights requirements first.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Leadville North?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Leadville North is 120 feet. The middle half runs from 73 to 162 feet. About 37% are under 100 feet, while 59% are between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 225 feet, but the deepest recorded well is 860 feet, showing that fractured bedrock can vary substantially.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Leadville North?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 120-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $7,800 to $12,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,800 to $24,000. Access, depth, casing, grout, and site conditions can change a bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Leadville North?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 12.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-five percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Ten percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. These figures come from 371 yield records and do not guarantee a new well’s production.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Leadville North?
faq.a: The map includes 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 3,848 historic mine features, and 14 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. That does not establish contamination at your property. Test an existing well and review local site history, especially near mining or cleanup locations. A permit alone does not certify that water is safe to drink.

faq.q: Are there water-level changes in Leadville North wells?
faq.a: Reported static water levels have a median of 70 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 54 to 110 feet. The median was 70 feet in the 2010s and 75 feet in the 2020s. That small shift indicates slightly deeper recent measurements, but only 88 wells report static levels, so the series does not prove a widespread declining water table.
